types.name: FAnimCurveKeyDef
types.doc:
One key of an authored scalar curve. Times are SECONDS in the sidecar

members.name: compression
members.doc:
How much error the quantizing codec may spend on THIS clip. One global
tolerance is wrong in both directions: a long root-motion track needs a
wider one to stay quantized at all, and a facial clip whose whole range
is a few millimetres needs a tighter one or the quantizer's step is
visible. Read by BOTH sites that compress — the `.mmodel` cook and the
clip load — through FAnimCompressionAuthoring. A tolerance of 0 means
"store this clip losslessly".

types.name: EAnimGraphNodeType
types.doc:
The pose-composition graph (UE's AnimGraph): a node network that composes
the runtime pieces that already exist — the state machine's inertialized
result, standalone clip players, per-bone layered blends, value-driven
pose switches and cached poses — into the final local pose. It lives on
the AnimationController and serializes inside the same .animgraph asset; an
empty or pass-through graph keeps the historical state-machine-only path
byte-for-byte identical.

members.name: Output
members.doc: 1 input: the final pose

members.name: StateMachine
members.doc: 0 inputs: the controller's state-machine pose (inertialized), supplied by the caller

members.name: Clip
members.doc: 0 inputs: standalone clip player with its own clock (clipName/speed/loop)

members.name: BlendByFloat
members.doc: 2 inputs A,B: alpha = clamp01((param - blendMin) / (blendMax - blendMin))

members.name: BlendByBool
members.doc: 2 inputs false,true: FBlendPosesByValue switch, timed by blendTime

members.name: LayeredBlend
members.doc: 2 inputs base,layer: FLayeredBlendPerBone; boneFilter = branch roots (bone + descendants); Additive reference = clipName sampled per basePoseMode, else bind pose; additiveType picks local vs mesh space

members.name: SavePose
members.doc: 1 input: stores the pose into slotName, passes it through

members.name: UsePose
members.doc: 0 inputs: reads slotName (this frame's store if already evaluated, else last frame's)

members.name: ExternalPose
members.doc: 1 input (fallback): pulls from FPoseProviderRegistry by slotName; a missing/declining provider yields the fallback

members.name: Mirror
members.doc: 1 input: reflects the pose through the FMirrorTable named by slotName

members.name: AimOffset
members.doc: 1 input: mesh-space additive from a 2D grid of aim poses, driven by (paramName, paramNameY)

members.name: BlendSpacePlayer
members.doc: 0 inputs: phase-matched 2D blend-space player with its own clock

members.name: SequenceEvaluator
members.doc: 0 inputs: clipName sampled at an EXPLICIT time (paramName), no clock of its own

members.name: RandomPlayer
members.doc: 0 inputs: plays one of clipNames, re-picking whenever the clip ends

members.name: ModifyBone
members.doc: 1 input: writes translation/rotation/scale onto boneName

members.name: CopyBone
members.doc: 1 input: copies sourceBoneName's channels onto boneName

members.name: LookAt
members.doc: 1 input: swings boneName's aimAxis onto a target point

members.name: TwoBoneIK
members.doc: 1 input: analytic root/mid/end solve onto a target point

members.name: OrientationWarp
members.doc: 1 input: yaws sourceBoneName and counter-yaws the boneFilter chain

members.name: Slot
members.doc: 1 input: composes the montage slot named by slotName over the source pose

members.name: StrideWarp
members.doc: 1 input: scales each leg's foot placement along the stride axis and re-solves the leg

members.name: SlopeWarp
members.doc: 1 input: plants the feet on a sloped ground plane and drops the pelvis to meet them

members.name: PoseByName
members.doc: 1 input: applies ONE named pose of the .pose at poseAssetPath, by layerWeight

members.name: PoseBlender
members.doc: 1 input: applies EVERY pose of the .pose, each weighted by the float parameter named after it

members.name: PoseDriver
members.doc: 1 input: RBF over sourceBoneName's rotation picks which of the .pose's poses fire

members.name: TwistCorrective
members.doc: 1 input: drives the twist bones in boneFilter by a share of sourceBoneName's roll about aimAxis

members.name: LinkedLayer
members.doc: 1 input: evaluates the graph the animator linked under slotName (UE linked anim layer), handing it this input; unlinked = pass-through

members.name: LayerInput
members.doc: 0 inputs: inside a linked layer graph, the pose the LinkedLayer node handed in (bind outside one)

types.name: EBoneModifyMode
types.doc:
What a skeletal-control node does to one transform channel. Ignore leaves
the incoming pose alone, which is why it is the default: a freshly added
ModifyBone must be a no-op until something is authored on it.

types.name: EAnimBoneSpace
types.doc:
The space a skeletal control reads and writes in. Component is the rig's own
accumulated space (the skeleton root transform excluded) — a bone written
there keeps its result no matter what its parents did, and its children ride
along, which is UE's ModifyBone/CopyBone component-space semantics.

members.name: clipName
members.doc:
Clip player; for LayeredBlend this is the OPTIONAL additive reference
clip (sampled per basePoseMode) — bind pose when empty.

members.name: clipId
members.doc:
The AnimSequence package of that clip. When set it wins over the name,
so renaming a clip or importing it under another mesh keeps the node on
it; FAnimGraph::BindClipIds fills it from the name once the clips load.

members.name: clipNames
members.doc:
RandomPlayer's candidate clips. Empty falls back to clipName, so a
RandomPlayer authored with a single clip behaves like a Clip node.

members.name: clipIds
members.doc: Package ids parallel to clipNames (an empty entry = by name only).

members.name: shuffle
members.doc: RandomPlayer: never draw the same clip twice in a row (UE's "shuffle").

members.name: paramName
members.doc: BlendByFloat / BlendByBool parameter (controller param namespace).

members.name: paramNameY
members.doc:
Second and third parameter names. Which node reads them is per type:
AimOffset and BlendSpacePlayer take (paramName, paramNameY) as their two
blend axes; LookAt and TwoBoneIK take all three as the target point's
X/Y/Z, and SlopeWarp as the ground NORMAL's X/Y/Z, all falling back to
the authored `translation` for any name left empty, so a fixed target (or
a fixed slope) needs no parameters at all. StrideWarp reads only
`paramName`, as its stride scale.

members.name: blendSpace
members.doc:
AimOffset / BlendSpacePlayer sample grid. AimOffset samples every entry
at time 0 (an aim offset is a pose, not a clip); BlendSpacePlayer runs
them on the node's own phase-matched clock.

members.name: boneName
members.doc:
Skeletal controls (ModifyBone / CopyBone / LookAt / TwoBoneIK /
OrientationWarp / StrideWarp / SlopeWarp). `boneName` is the bone
written; `sourceBoneName` is CopyBone's source, TwoBoneIK's root and the
warping nodes' pelvis; `endBoneName` is TwoBoneIK's effector.
`layerWeight` doubles as the control's alpha, so a control eases in
through the field the rest of the graph already uses for weight.

members.name: rotationEuler
members.doc: degrees

members.name: aimAxis
members.doc: LookAt: the bone-local axis pointed at the target

members.name: upAxis
members.doc: OrientationWarp: the axis yawed about

members.name: hasLimit
members.doc:
Angle cap, in degrees, on whatever the node swings: LookAt's swing,
OrientationWarp's yaw, and TwoBoneIK's mid-joint interior angle (which
uses BOTH bounds — 0 fully folded, 180 straight). Off by default so a
node added and left alone solves exactly as it did before limits existed.

members.name: strideScale
members.doc:
StrideWarp: how far each foot's offset from the pelvis is scaled ALONG
the stride axis (`aimAxis`, projected onto the plane normal to `upAxis`
so a warp can never lift or sink a foot). `paramName` overrides it per
frame — that is where a locomotion system publishes
desiredSpeed / animationSpeed. 1 leaves the clip's own stride alone.

members.name: warpPelvisAdjust
members.doc:
StrideWarp / SlopeWarp: how far the pelvis may drop, in skeleton units,
to meet feet the warp put out of the legs' reach (a lengthened stride) or
below where they were (the downhill foot on a slope). 0 (the default)
leaves the pelvis alone, so a freshly added node only moves feet and the
author opts into the body following them.

members.name: twistScale
members.doc:
TwistCorrective: how much of the source bone's roll the LAST twist bone
in boneFilter receives (1 = all of it). With `twistRamp` the bones share
it in even steps (1/N, 2/N, …), which is what an upperarm→forearm twist
chain wants; off, every bone gets the full scaled roll.

members.name: poseAssetPath
members.doc:
PoseByName / PoseBlender / PoseDriver: the `.pose` this node reads,
resolved through FPoseAssetLibrary. A pose asset is bulk data shared
across controllers, so the graph carries the PATH and never a copy.

members.name: poseName
members.doc:
PoseByName: which pose of that asset is applied. PoseBlender ignores it —
it reads every pose, each weighted by the float parameter named after it
(prefixed by `paramName` when one is authored, which is how two blenders
on one asset stay in separate parameter namespaces).

members.name: driverRadius
members.doc:
PoseDriver: how far, in degrees, the driver bone may sit from a pose's
own rotation and still contribute. The default is wide enough that a
freshly dropped driver visibly does something on a rig it fits, because a
driver that silently fires nothing reads as broken rather than untuned.

members.name: driverNormalize
members.doc:
Normalized weights make the targets a partition (two half-matched poses
read as one pose); unnormalized lets genuinely independent shapes stack.

members.name: blendProfileName
members.doc:
A controller blend profile applied to this node's per-bone weights
(LayeredBlend / BlendByFloat / BlendByBool). TimeFactor profiles are
ignored here — they describe a window, and these blends have no clock.

members.name: blendType
members.doc: LayeredBlend.

members.name: additiveType
members.doc: Additive composition space — see EAdditiveType (AnimGraphNodes.h).

members.name: basePoseMode
members.doc:
Additive reference extraction. The AnimationFrame default with
basePoseTime 0 reproduces the historical clipName@t0 behavior, so
legacy assets load unchanged. AnimationScaled phase-matches the
reference against the layer input's clip clock when that input is a
Clip node; any other input shape falls back to basePoseTime.

members.name: blendDepth
members.doc:
LayeredBlend: how many bones down from each branch root the layer
ramps in (UE's blend depth) — 0 or 1 = full weight at the root, N = the
root at 1/N, its child at 2/N, ... full from the N-th bone. A spine
layer with depth 3 eases in over three vertebrae instead of snapping
the whole torso at the first one.

members.name: meshSpaceRotationBlend
members.doc:
LayeredBlend (override): blend rotations in component space instead of
bone-local space (UE's mesh-space rotation blend), so an upper-body
aim keeps pointing where it was authored to whatever the pelvis does.

members.name: boneFilter
members.doc:
Branch-root bone names: a bone is in the layer when it IS one of these
or descends from one. Empty = the whole skeleton. OrientationWarp reads
it as its ordered counter-yaw spine chain, and StrideWarp / SlopeWarp as
their list of FOOT bones — each foot's leg is the two bones above it, so
one name per leg describes the whole chain.

members.name: slotName
members.doc:
SavePose / UsePose slot; for ExternalPose this is the registered
pose-provider name (FPoseProviderRegistry), for Mirror the name of one of
the controller's FMirrorTables, for Slot the montage slot
(AnimatorComponent::montageSlots), for LinkedLayer the layer name
(AnimatorComponent::linkedLayers) — same serialized field throughout.

members.name: fromNode
members.doc: source node (single output pin)

types.name: FAnimGraphCompiledNode
types.doc:
One node's resolved wiring: input node INDICES per pin, its fan-out, and
every bone name it authored turned into a bone index. Resolved once per
(graph structure, skeleton) instead of per frame, so the evaluator never
compares a string on the hot path — a branch filter used to walk the whole
skeleton against its name list every evaluation.

members.name: filterBones
members.doc: boneFilter in authored order, unknown names dropped.

members.name: branchMask
members.doc:
Branch-root membership (1 = the bone is a filter bone or descends from
one; all ones when the filter is empty). Scaled by layerWeight at
evaluation, so a weight edit needs no recompile.

members.name: sourceBindRotation
members.doc: Bind local rotations of sourceBone and filterBones (TwistCorrective).

members.name: graph
members.doc:
Two graphs can share a version number (every graph starts at 1), so a
controller swap is caught by identity as well.

types.name: FAnimGraphEvalScratch
types.doc:
Every buffer an evaluation needs, kept across frames so the capacity is
paid once per entity: the per-node pose slots (the memo), the bind pose,
and the rig / reference / weight scratch the node bodies used to allocate
on every call.

members.name: previewProfiles
members.doc:
Where an instance-less (preview) evaluation keeps its resolved blend
profiles and pose assets; a real animator caches them on its instance.

types.name: FAnimGraphInstance
types.doc:
Per-entity runtime state. Lives on the AnimatorComponent so a controller
asset shared across entities never shares clocks; keyed by node id so an
editor graph edit (add/remove nodes) leaves surviving nodes' state alone.

members.name: mirrorCache
members.doc:
Mirror tables resolved against THIS entity's skeleton. Resolution is
per-instance rather than cached on the shared FMirrorTable because
animation evaluates on job workers and a controller asset is shared by
every entity playing it.

members.name: savedPoses
members.doc:
SavePose slots persist across frames: a UsePose evaluated BEFORE its
SavePose this frame reads last frame's pose (UE cached-pose semantics).

members.name: compiled
members.doc:
The graph's wiring and bone names resolved against THIS entity's
skeleton (rebuilt when the graph's structure version or the skeleton
changes), and the pose buffers the evaluator reuses frame to frame.

members.name: blendProfileCache
members.doc:
Blend profiles resolved against THIS entity's skeleton, keyed by profile
name rather than by node so two nodes naming one profile resolve it once.
Per-instance for the same reason the mirror cache is.

members.name: poseAssetCache
members.doc:
Pose assets resolved against THIS entity's skeleton, keyed by `.pose`
path so a PoseByName and the PoseDriver feeding it resolve the same asset
once. Per-instance for the same reason the mirror cache is.

members.name: poseAssetsPrimed
members.doc:
Set once this instance's graph has had its `.pose` files pulled into the
library on the GAME thread. The evaluator can load one itself, but it
runs on job workers, and a first-touch VFS read there is a file system
hit inside the parallel animation phase.

members.name: linkedInstances
members.doc:
One instance per linked layer name: a linked graph keeps its own clip
clocks and cached poses. `linkedGraph` is the graph it last ran, so
relinking another graph under the name starts its state fresh.

members.name: choice
members.doc:
RandomPlayer: the drawn index into clipNames and this instance's own
draw sequence. Seeded from the node id so two entities on the same
graph do not march in lockstep, and so a replay of the same entity
draws the same clips.

members.name: statePose
members.doc: The state machine's finished pose for StateMachine nodes (null = bind).

members.name: mirrorTables
members.doc:
Mirror tables the Mirror node can name (the controller's own set). Null
or a missing name makes the node a pass-through rather than an error —
a graph mid-edit still evaluates.

members.name: blendProfiles
members.doc:
Blend profiles a node's `blendProfileName` can address (the controller's
own set). Null or a missing name leaves the blend on its plain weights,
which is the pre-profile behaviour and what a mid-edit graph needs.

members.name: montageSlots
members.doc:
This frame's montage-slot overlays, ticked and sampled before the graph
runs. A Slot node claims the entry it names (marks it consumed) whether
or not it had weight to contribute — the node's presence is the
statement that the graph owns where that slot lands, so the post-graph
composition must never apply it again. Null leaves every Slot node a
pass-through, which is what a preview evaluation wants.

members.name: linkedLayers
members.signature: const std::unordered_map<std::string, std::shared_ptr<const FAnimGraph>>* linkedLayers = nullptr
members.doc:
Graphs linked into named layers on this animator (LinkedLayer nodes),
and inside one of them the pose its LinkedLayer node handed in.

members.name: structureVersion
members.doc:
Bumped by every mutator here (and by Deserialize / CopyFrom). An
instance's compiled wiring is keyed on it, so an editor that edits
`nodes` / `links` directly must call MarkStructureDirty() — a bone
name changed in place would otherwise keep resolving to the old index.

members.name: HasWork
members.doc:
True when evaluating would change the pose: an Output node exists and
its input chain is more than a bare StateMachine node.

members.name: AddNode
members.signature: uint64_t AddNode(EAnimGraphNodeType type, const Vec2& pos)

members.name: Connect
members.signature: uint64_t Connect(uint64_t fromNode, uint64_t toNode, uint32_t toSlot)
members.doc: Replaces any existing link into (toNode, toSlot). Returns the link id.

members.name: PrimePoseAssets
members.doc:
Pulls every `.pose` this graph names into FPoseAssetLibrary. Call it
from the game thread before evaluating: the evaluator will load one
itself, but it runs on job workers and the first touch would be a file
read inside the parallel phase.

members.name: BindClipIds
members.doc:
Fills every clip reference's package id (Clip, Sequence Evaluator,
Random Player candidates, additive reference, blend-space samples) from
the clip its name resolves to, and leaves an id that already resolves
alone. Game thread, like the controller's own ResolveClips: a saved
graph then carries the ids forward. Returns how many ids it wrote.

members.name: Evaluate
members.signature: bool Evaluate(const FAnimGraphContext& ctx, std::vector<Mat4>& out) const
members.doc:
Evaluate the graph into `out` (local transforms, skeleton bone order).
Nodes are memoized per call, so a node feeding two inputs evaluates —
and advances its clock — exactly once per frame. Returns false when
there is nothing to evaluate (no skeleton / no output node).

MDF <-> graph, as "GraphNode"/"GraphLink" children of the given parent

types.name: EAdditiveType
types.doc:
How an additive delta composes onto the base (UE's EAdditiveAnimationType).
LocalSpace multiplies the delta rotation into each bone's local rotation.
MeshSpace measures and applies the ROTATION delta in component space —
after the base's accumulated mesh-space rotation — so an aim offset or a
recoil authored against one stance stays world-correct layered over any
base pose; translation and scale deltas stay local in both modes, matching
UE's mesh-space rotation additive.

types.name: EAdditiveBasePoseMode
types.doc:
Where the additive reference (base) pose comes from (UE's
EAdditiveBasePoseType). ReferencePose ignores any reference clip and
measures the delta from the skeleton bind pose. AnimationFrame samples the
reference clip at a fixed time. AnimationScaled samples it at the layer
clip's normalized phase scaled into the reference clip's length, so a
looping additive stays aligned with a looping source of another duration.

types.name: FMontageSlotPose
types.doc:
One montage slot's overlay for THIS frame: its playhead already advanced
and its pose already sampled, BEFORE the pose graph runs, so a Slot node
can compose it at the point in the graph the author put it. `consumed` is
what stops the post-graph composition applying the same overlay a second
time — a slot a graph never mentions still lands on top of the final pose,
which is how montages behaved before Slot nodes existed. `active` says a
montage is playing on the slot at all; the map itself is reused scratch, so
a stale key from a previously evaluated entity must not read as a slot.

members.name: boneMask
members.doc: empty = the whole skeleton

members.signature: static void BlendAdditiveWeighted(const std::vector<Mat4>& base, const std::vector<Mat4>& layer, const std::vector<Mat4>& reference, const std::vector<float>& perBoneWeight, std::vector<Mat4>& out)

members.name: BlendAdditiveMeshSpaceWeighted
members.signature: static void BlendAdditiveMeshSpaceWeighted(const std::vector<Mat4>& base, const std::vector<Mat4>& layer, const std::vector<Mat4>& reference, const std::vector<float>& perBoneWeight, const Skeleton& skeleton, std::vector<Mat4>& out)
members.doc:
Mesh-space additive: rotation deltas are measured between the layer and
reference poses' ACCUMULATED (component-space) rotations and applied
after the base's accumulated rotation, then the whole pose is converted
back to local space through the modified parents. An unweighted bone
therefore keeps its component-space orientation even when an ancestor
took the delta — the property that makes look-ats/recoil layer correctly
over arbitrary bases. Needs the skeleton for parent indices; deltas are
measured inside the rig (Skeleton root transform excluded, which cancels
because all three poses share it).

types.name: EAnimGraphPropType
types.doc:
How one authored field of FAnimGraphNode is stored. The set is deliberately
small: everything a pose node exposes is a number, a flag, a name, a list of
names, a vector or a fixed choice — plus the one blend grid, which is the
only field with a shape of its own.

members.name: Reference
members.doc:
A string that NAMES something else rather than holding a value: a
`.pose` on disk, a mirror table declared beside the graph. The kind
exists so the inspector can offer the things that exist and mark a name
that resolves to none of them, instead of leaving an author to type a
path blind and find out at run time.

types.name: EAnimGraphNodeStyle
types.doc:
What ROLE a node kind plays. The registry lives in the runtime module and
must never name an editor colour, so it names the role and the panel maps
roles onto Arc style tokens exactly once instead of once per kind.

types.name: TAnimGraphEnumAccess
types.doc:
A pointer-to-member per storage kind rather than one byte offset:
FAnimGraphNode holds std::vector and std::string members and so is not
standard-layout, which makes offsetof on it only conditionally supported.

members.doc:
Where a Reference row's candidates come from. A value starting with '.'

types.name: EAnimTrackFormat
types.doc:
How one track (translation / rotation / scale of one bone) is stored.
Quantized is the normal case; Raw is the lossless fallback taken when the
measured error of the quantized form exceeds the caller's tolerance — a
long root-motion track whose range is tens of metres will land there, and
silently shipping a visibly-wrong bone is worse than spending the bytes.
Values above FAnimTrackCodec::kPackedFormatBase are bit-packed tracks (the
variable bit rate): the value minus the base is the bits per component.

types.name: FAnimQuantizedVectorKey
types.doc:
Quantized vector key: time as a fraction of the track's own time span,
each axis as a fraction of that axis's own range. 8 bytes against the
16 a raw PositionKey costs.

types.name: FAnimQuantizedRotationKey
types.doc:
Quantized rotation key: time plus a 48-bit smallest-three quaternion.
8 bytes against the 20 a raw RotationKey costs.

types.name: FAnimVectorKeyIn
types.doc:
Lossless input/output form. The codec speaks these rather than
AnimationClip's PositionKey/RotationKey so the cook side can call it
without including a dllexported runtime header.

types.name: FCompressedAnimTrack
types.doc:
Everything needed to decode one track without touching any other track:
the format, the key count, where the keys start in the owning blob, and
the two affine ranges (time, value) the quantized words are fractions of.

types.name: FAnimBoneTolerance
types.doc:
One per-bone budget: bones whose name matches `bone` compress at these
tolerances instead of the clip's. `bone` is an exact name or a pattern
with a leading and/or trailing `*` ("*Finger*", "jaw*", "*_end"). A
negative tolerance means "keep the clip's value" for that track, so an
entry can tighten rotation alone. First match in list order wins — put
the specific entries before the broad ones.

members.name: translationTolerance
members.doc:
Tolerances are the largest end-to-end error the caller will accept from
the quantized form, measured against the ORIGINAL keys — not a promise
about the quantizer's step size. A track that misses gets stored raw.

members.name: collapseConstantTracks
members.doc:
A track whose every key sits within tolerance of its first key collapses
to a single key. Rigs are full of these — nearly every bone has a
constant scale, and most have a constant translation — and it is where
most of the real saving comes from.

members.name: boneOverrides
members.doc:
Per-bone budgets. Fingers and the face want a tighter rotation budget
than the clip (their small ranges make the quantizer's step visible),
a prop bone or an end effector nobody sees can take a looser one.

members.name: kPackedFormatBase
members.doc:
Variable bit rate, per track (ACL's per-track bit rates): a quantized
track that still meets its tolerance with fewer than 16 bits per
component is bit-packed at the narrowest width that does. The width
rides in the format byte, kPackedFormatBase + bits, so neither the .mmodel
channel header nor a cooked descriptor grows a field. A packed vector key
is a 16-bit time word plus three `bits`-wide axes; a packed rotation key
is the time word, the 2-bit largest-component index and three
`bits`-wide smallest-three components.

components over [-1/sqrt(2), +1/sqrt(2)] — 47 bits, written as 6 bytes.
The sign is folded away by flipping q so the largest component is
positive, which costs nothing (q and -q are the same rotation).

the leader instead of drifting after the entry sync. Leader states
report their phase back through UpdateResult for the system to
publish. Null keeps the historical per-controller entry-sync.

sync. When both the leader and the follower carry the named pair the
follower pins to the marker; otherwise it falls back to the phase map,
which is what every clip without markers keeps doing.

types.name: EBlendProfileMode
types.doc:
What the per-bone number in a blend profile MEANS. The three modes are UE's,
and they are genuinely different questions: TimeFactor stretches the blend
WINDOW per bone (the legs finish a transition while the torso is still
catching up), WeightFactor stretches the per-bone PROGRESS inside one shared
window, and BlendMask states outright how much of the incoming pose a bone
takes at all.

types.name: FBlendProfileEntry
types.doc:
One authored row. `includeChildren` is the branch-root form the layered-blend
bone filter already uses: naming a spine and taking the subtree is how a rig
is actually authored, and spelling out every finger is how that authoring
silently rots the first time a bone is added.

types.name: FBlendProfileResolved
types.doc:
A profile resolved against one skeleton. Kept per ANIMATOR INSTANCE for the
same reason FMirrorResolved is: a controller asset is shared by every entity
playing it and animation evaluates on job workers, so a cache hanging off the
shared asset would be written from several threads at once.

types.name: FBlendProfile
types.doc:
The blend profile (UE's UBlendProfile): a named per-bone scale that a
transition, a layered blend or a value blend applies on top of its own
weight. Pure data — resolution against a skeleton is a static, so one profile
can drive any number of skeletons without holding state for any of them.

members.name: DefaultValue
members.doc:
Unlisted bones read 1.0 under TimeFactor/WeightFactor (an unmentioned
bone blends exactly as it would with no profile at all) and 0.0 under
BlendMask (a mask is a statement about what participates, so silence
there has to mean "not this one").

the end), BlendMask scales the weight itself and so really can hold a
bone back permanently, and TimeFactor is a no-op here — it has nothing to
say about a blend that is not on a clock.

by `weight`, mirroring how the pose and anim curves compose. Consumers

the capsule up) instead of leaving it in the pose and zeroing the
delta's Y. Off by default: idle/walk clips bob the root, and without
this flag that bob stays cosmetic in the pose.

playhead alone (weight-scaled), so locomotion blends can never feed
the capsule — montage-driven attacks/dodges still do. Slot montages
are not sourced, only the main montage player.

the scale a dual quaternion cannot carry. Dual-quaternion skinning blends
rigid motions on the rotation manifold, so a wrist twisted 180° keeps its
volume where linear blend skinning collapses it to a candy wrapper; the
price is that scale has to ride alongside and be blended linearly.

real, row 1 = dual, row 2 = scale, row 3 = 0,0,0,1) and the draw's bone
base carries a flag bit telling every skinned pass which encoding its
records use. Blend() mirrors Common/Skinning.hlsli exactly so a test can
pin the shader's arithmetic without a GPU.

Bases stay far below 2^31 (the arena is a few thousand slots), and the
bit survives every push site unchanged, which is what lets one upload
decide the encoding for the G-Buffer, shadow, velocity, selection and
pre-skin passes at once.

types.name: EIKJointConstraint
types.doc:
Description of an N-bone chain solved iteratively by FABRIK (Forward And
Backward Reaching Inverse Kinematics).

`bones` lists bone indices from root → end, contiguous along the parent
chain. The solver does NOT verify they form an actual parent chain — it
just treats them as a kinematic chain with the segment lengths inferred
from the current bind/animated pose. Author-side responsibility to keep
the list ordered and connected.

Typical use cases (chains longer than 3 bones, where the analytical
two-bone solver doesn't apply):
- spine bending (pelvis → chest → neck)
- tail / tentacle / cable
- multi-finger phalanx
- prehensile limb (creature animation)

`polePosition` is an optional swing hint applied AFTER the FABRIK pass:
the chain is rotated around the root→end axis so the middle joint(s)
face toward the pole. This is the only joint-orientation control we
expose — FABRIK itself only constrains positions.

`maxIterations` / `tolerance` cap the solver work; in practice 5-10
iterations converge to within 1mm for human-scale chains.
What a joint is allowed to do to the segment leaving it.

None    — unconstrained, the classic positions-only FABRIK behaviour.
Hinge   — one degree of freedom: the outgoing segment is forced into the
plane perpendicular to `hingeAxis` and its swing about that axis
is clamped to [minAngleDegrees, maxAngleDegrees]. This is the
knee/elbow case, and the reason it matters is that unconstrained
FABRIK will happily fold a knee forwards.
Cone    — the outgoing segment stays within `coneAngleDegrees` of the
incoming one. Shoulders, hips, tail segments.

types.name: FIKJointLimit
types.doc:
Angles are measured against the direction ARRIVING at the joint (the
previous segment), except at the chain root, where the reference is the
root's own outgoing direction in the pre-solve animated pose — there is no
previous segment there, and using the parent bone's axis instead would make
the limit depend on rig conventions the solver cannot see.

`hingeAxis` is in the same space the solver runs in (component space of the
pose it was handed), not bone-local.

types.name: EIKChainSolver
types.doc:
How an N-bone chain reaches its target.

FABRIK  — positions first, rotations reconstructed after; smooth, spreads
the bend evenly along the chain (spines, tails).
CCD     — Cyclic Coordinate Descent: joint by joint from the tip, each
rotated to swing the end toward the target. Bends the joints
nearest the end first, which is what a curling finger, a
tentacle tip or a mechanical arm wants, and honours the same
hinge / cone limits per joint.

members.name: jointLimits
members.doc:
Index-parallel with `bones`; entry i limits the segment from bone i to
bone i+1. Empty (or shorter than `bones`) means unconstrained — the
missing entries are not an error, they are the default.

types.name: FABRIK
types.doc:
FABRIK solver. Iterative, positions-only, then converts to bone rotations.

Algorithm (per iteration):
1. Backward pass: place end at target. For i = end-1 .. root, snap
each joint to a distance `len[i]` toward the next joint.
2. Forward pass: snap root back to its original position. For i = root+1
.. end, snap each joint to `len[i-1]` away from the previous joint.
3. Stop when |end - target| < tolerance or maxIterations reached.

Joint limits, when present, are enforced inside the FORWARD pass — the one
that runs last and therefore owns the final positions. Constraining the
backward pass too would fight the target and stall convergence; letting the
forward pass clamp means an over-constrained chain simply stops short of an
unreachable target instead of tearing. The pole hint runs after the solve
and rotates the whole chain rigidly about the root→end axis, so it cannot
break a cone limit (those are relative angles) but CAN swing a hinge out of
its plane — a hinge already fixes the bend plane, so setting both on the
same joint is authoring two answers to one question.

After convergence we compute new world rotations: for each non-end joint,
the rotation that takes (next-bone-pos in old pose) to (next-bone-pos in
new pose). Optional pole hint applies a swing-around-root→end rotation so
the middle of the chain faces the pole.

types.name: FFullBodyIKEffector
types.doc:
One thing the body is being asked to reach. Unlike an IKGoal or a FABRIKGoal
this does NOT name a chain: the chain is whatever lies between the solver's
root and this bone, which is the entire point — two effectors sharing a spine
negotiate over it instead of the second one overwriting the first.

members.name: positionWeight
members.doc:
How hard this effector pulls at a joint it shares with another. A hand
reaching for a ledge at 1.0 and one steadying a rail at 0.2 bend the
spine mostly toward the ledge, which is the whole reason a whole-body
solve is not N independent chains.

types.name: FFullBodyIKBoneSetting
types.doc:
Per-bone resistance. 0 leaves the joint free, 1 pins it where the animation
put it. A stiff chest is how a reach reads as a reach and not as a character
folding in half — a positions-only solver has no other way to say that some
joints should give before others.

members.name: limit
members.doc:
How far the solve may turn the segment ARRIVING at this bone (parent →
bone) away from where the animation had it, measured in the frame the
parent's own segment moved to — so a limit says "this joint may bend 30°
more than the clip did", whatever the rig's rest pose looks like. Cone
caps the angle; Hinge keeps the segment in the plane normal to
`hingeAxis` (component space of the animated pose, carried along with
the parent) and clamps its signed swing to [min, max].

members.name: rootBone
members.doc:
The bone the whole solve hangs from — the pelvis on a biped. Every
effector must be a descendant of it; one that is not is skipped rather
than silently solved against the wrong ancestor.

members.name: rootIsPinned
members.doc:
A pinned root stays exactly where the animation put it (a character
standing and reaching). Unpinned, the body itself drifts toward the
effectors, which is what a hang, a swing or a ragdoll-assisted reach
needs — and the only case where this solver writes a TRANSLATION.

members.name: weight
members.doc:
Whole-solver alpha, so a full-body pass can ease in the same way every
other node in this module does.

members.name: refineBranches
members.doc:
After the tree solve, re-solve each effector's own limb below the
nearest joint it shares with another effector (UE PBIK's per-bone
offsets, in effect): the shared joint keeps its averaged rotation and
the limb takes up the residual, so the hand lands ON the ledge instead
of near it. A limb with a joint limit on it keeps the tree result.

types.name: FFullBodyIK
types.doc:
UE's Full Body IK, as a multi-effector FABRIK over the skeleton TREE rather
than over one chain.

The chain solver already here cannot express this: run it twice for two arms
and the second solve overwrites the spine the first one bent, so the body
snaps between the two targets frame to frame depending on the order. The tree
form fixes that by making a shared joint the weighted average of what each
effector's backward pass wants from it — the classic multi-effector FABRIK
sub-base rule — and only then running one forward pass outward from the root.

Positions-only, like FABRIK: rotations are reconstructed at the end from the
direction each bone's children moved. Because every segment length is
preserved through the solve, writing rotations alone reproduces the solved
positions exactly, and the root's translation is the single exception (it
only moves when the root is unpinned).

The one place that reconstruction is approximate is a BRANCHING joint: a
chest pulled two ways has one rotation and two children asking for different
ones, so it gets the weighted average and the effectors below it would land
near their targets rather than on them. `refineBranches` closes that gap by
re-solving each effector's limb below its branching joint with the chain
solver, which is what PBIK's per-bone rotation offsets buy UE. Joint limits
(`FFullBodyIKBoneSetting::limit`) are enforced in the forward pass, the one
that owns the final positions; a limited limb is not refined.

types.name: TwoBoneIKChain
types.doc:
Description of a three-bone chain that gets solved analytically.

Typical mapping:
arm:  rootBone = shoulder, midBone = elbow,  endBone = wrist
leg:  rootBone = hip,      midBone = knee,   endBone = ankle

`polePosition` is the world-space hint that tells the solver which way the
mid joint should face (e.g. for a knee, put the pole in front of the
character so it doesn't fold backward). It is applied as a swing about the
root→end axis AFTER the chain has been solved onto the target, so it moves
the knee without ever moving the foot off its goal. When `hasPoleHint` is
false the solver bends in the chain's current plane — fine for "preserve
silhouette" use cases (foot-IK on flat ground), but knee/elbow direction
is then determined entirely by the current animated pose.

`weight` is a 0..1 slerp blend between the pre-IK and post-IK pose; lets
gameplay code ease the constraint in and out without popping.

members.name: hasMidLimit
members.doc:
Range the MIDDLE joint's interior angle (root-mid-end) is allowed to take,
in degrees: 0 is fully folded, 180 dead straight. The pole hint decides
which SIDE the joint bends toward; nothing until now decided how FAR, so a
target placed behind a knee hyperextended it into a backwards leg and a
target on top of the hip folded the shin through the thigh.

Off by default — an existing chain solves exactly as it did. When on, the
reach is recomputed from the clamped angle, so an out-of-range target is
approached as closely as the limit allows (the direction align still
points the limb at it) instead of being reached by breaking the joint.

members.name: allowTwist
members.doc:
UE's bAllowTwist, and it only means anything on the target-rotation
overload. A target rotation is authored from something that measured a
DIRECTION and nothing else — a floor normal says which way is up under
the foot, it says nothing about which way the toes point; a grip normal
says which way the palm faces. Taking such a rotation whole overwrites
the twist about the limb's own axis too, so a foot planted on a slope
yaws off the direction the animation was walking in and a hand rolls on
its wrist. With twist disallowed only the SWING of the override is
applied and the animated twist survives underneath it.

Defaults to the historical whole-rotation behaviour so an explicitly
authored goal (a hand placed on a ladder rung, where the twist IS the
point) keeps solving exactly as it did.

types.name: TwoBoneIK
types.doc:
Two-bone IK solver. Analytical, single-iteration, runs in O(1).

Algorithm (law of cosines on the triangle root-mid-end):
1. Forward-kinematics pass over `localTransforms` to get world space.
2. Compute current bend angle at mid bone.
3. Compute desired bend angle from target distance via cos rule.
4. Rotate at midBone by Δangle around the chain's plane normal so the
chain reaches the target distance. Δangle is current-minus-desired:
opening the angle BETWEEN the segments shrinks the interior angle at
the joint, so the two run opposite ways.
5. Rotate at rootBone so the end-effector direction points at the target.
6. With a pole hint, swing the solved chain about the root→end axis so the
mid joint faces the pole. That axis passes through the effector, so this
step cannot pull the end bone off the target it just reached.
7. Optionally override the end bone's rotation (target orientation —
e.g. align foot to floor normal, or wrist to a grip).

Outputs are written back into `localTransforms` for the root, mid, and
optionally end bone, preserving each bone's translation + scale.

types.name: FPoseAsset
types.doc:
The `.pose` asset (UE's UPoseAsset): a set of named poses over a shared bone
list, applied either as deltas from a base pose (the normal case — a
corrective, a facial shape, a hand grip) or as full local transforms.

It is a FILE and not a child of the `.animgraph` on purpose. A mirror table is
fifty short name pairs and belongs inside the graph document; a pose asset is
one transform per tracked bone per pose, is shared by several controllers,
and inlining it would copy the bulk into every graph that names it and make
the `.animgraph` diff unreadable. It is pure data — resolution against a skeleton
is a static — so one asset drives any number of skeletons.

The RBF targets are NOT a second authored list: each pose in the asset
already stores that driver bone's rotation, so the pose IS its own target.
That is UE's "copy target rotations from pose asset" made the only path —
a separately authored target list is a second copy of the same rotations,
and the two drift the moment a pose is re-exported.

types.name: FRetargetAsset
types.doc:
The authored `.retarget` — UE's IK Retargeter asset. It carries what the
runtime FRetargetOptions carries (the name map, the prefix strips, the
translation modes and the chains) plus what only an authoring surface can
hold: which two skeletons the pair was built for, the root's travel rules,
per-chain FK/IK switches and the retarget poses.

The file it writes is the same MDF document FRetargetSerializer reads — the
mapping nodes keep their v1 names and shapes, and the additions sit beside
them — so a scene's RetargetComponent keeps resolving an asset this editor
saved. Everything past the mapping (root mode, FK gating, the poses) is
honoured by the evaluation here and by the export; the runtime map has no
seam for them yet.

Every list is serialized SORTED by its key: two of the tables were hash
maps before this asset existed, and a file whose bytes reshuffle between
saves defeats both the undo dedupe and the round-trip check.

Retargeter minus the IK chains.

name map for a real rig is dozens of pairs plus the prefix strips plus the
per-bone translation modes, and it is a property of the SOURCE-to-TARGET

the same two rigs re-declares it, and the first one to be edited without the

writes their entries SORTED by key. An asset whose bytes shuffle between
saves shows up as a diff in every commit that touched anything nearby, and
the round-trip test could not compare text at all.

types.name: ERetargetTranslationMode
types.doc:
How a matched bone's TRANSLATION retargets (UE's per-bone modes):
Skeleton         target rest position — bone lengths belong to the
target rig (the safe default for humanoids).
Animation        the source's animated local position verbatim —
facial rigs / squash-and-stretch where the
translation IS the animation.
AnimationScaled  source animated position × the rigs' height ratio —
root-style travel on a differently-sized rig.

types.name: FRetargetChain
types.doc:
Name-matching rules applied before exact-name lookup, in order:
1. explicit `nameMap` (source bone name → target bone name),
2. prefix strips on BOTH sides ("mixamorig:" → ""), then exact match.
Per-bone translation modes are keyed by TARGET bone name; unlisted
bones use `defaultTranslation` (the root keeps its height-scaled path
regardless — that behavior predates the modes and montages rely on it).
A named limb whose END EFFECTOR has to land in the same PLACE — scaled by
the rigs' proportions — and not merely at the same joint angles.

Rotation-only retargeting is exact when the target rig is a uniform scale of
the source. It is not, in general: give the target a longer upper arm and a
shorter forearm of the same total reach and the replayed angles put its hand
somewhere else entirely. That is what breaks hands on props, feet on stairs
and weapon grips — the cases where the POSITION is the animation.

members.doc: e.g. the source rig's shoulder

members.name: sourceEndBone
members.doc: ... and its hand

members.name: weight
members.doc:
0 = pure rotation retarget (what happens without a chain), 1 = the
effector is placed. In between, the goal is blended toward the placed
position, so a rig can be eased onto chain retargeting.

types.name: FRetargetMap
types.doc:
Animation retargeting — replays a pose authored on one skeleton
onto another with the same (or partially matching) bone NAMES but
different proportions and rest orientations.

Per matched bone the source's local rotation is expressed as a delta
from its own rest pose and re-applied over the TARGET's rest pose:
targetLocalRot = targetRestRot * (srcRestRot^-1 * srcLocalRot)
Translations always stay the target's rest values (bone lengths are a
property of the target rig), except the root whose animated offset is
scaled by the rigs' height ratio so walk cycles don't foot-slide.

members.name: SetLodBonesToRemove
members.signature: void SetLodBonesToRemove(uint32_t lod, const std::vector<std::string>& boneNames)
members.doc:
A distant character does not need its finger, jaw or twist bones
animated: the pixels those bones move are smaller than the error. Naming
a bone here excludes it AND its whole subtree from evaluation at that
LOD and every coarser one — a child cannot be animated by a parent that
is not, and UE's authoring model is the same "remove this branch".

An excluded bone is not deleted: it keeps its BIND local transform, so
its subtree still rides its parent rigidly and the palette keeps its
length. That is what makes this safe to switch per frame — nothing
downstream (skinning matrices, sockets, attachment) changes shape.

LOD 0 is always fully required; a level that was never authored inherits
the closest coarser one that was, so a mesh with masks at 1 and 3 does
the right thing at 2 without the caller repeating itself.

members.name: AddVirtualBone
members.signature: int32_t AddVirtualBone(const std::string& name, const std::string& sourceBone, const std::string& targetBone)
members.doc:
An IK goal or an aim point that lives in one bone's space but sits where
another bone is — a hand target under the spine, a weapon point under
the head — without re-authoring the skeleton in a DCC. The bone is
appended after every real bone and carries no skin weights, so the skin
palette, the clip bindings and every existing index stay valid. Its drive
happens inside ComputeGlobalTransforms, the one hierarchy walk every pose
consumer (animation system, anim graph, control rig, retargeting, the
editors' previews) goes through, so it follows Target on every frame of
every one of them.

-1 when the name is empty or taken, a bone is missing, source equals
target, or the skeleton is at the bone limit.

members.name: RemoveVirtualBones
members.doc:
Drops every virtual bone and keeps the imported rig. The object stays
the one the level's animators share, so a re-authored set can be laid
onto it in place; a pose buffer sized for the old count is resized by
the next ComputeGlobalTransforms.
